I had a train to catch on Saturday morning.
The train left at nine o'clock, and I planned to arrive early.
I packed my bag the night before, so I wouldn't forget anything important.
I woke up on time, but I moved slowly.
I made coffee, ate breakfast, and checked my phone too many times.
By the time I left home, I was already a little late for my plan.
I walked fast to the train station.
It usually takes fifteen minutes, but I tried to walk faster than usual.
My bag felt heavier than I remembered, and my shoulder started to hurt.
I reached the station at five minutes to nine.
I looked at the big board for my platform number.
My train was on platform six, and I ran toward the stairs as fast as I could.
I ran down the stairs and onto the platform.
I could see the train doors, but they were already closing.
I waved my hand, but the doors didn't open again for me.
The train slowly pulled away from the platform.
I stood there, out of breath, and watched it go.
I had missed it by less than one minute, which felt almost unfair.
I felt annoyed with myself.
I checked the board again for the next train.
The next one wasn't for another hour, and I had nothing to do at the station.
I found a bench and sat down.
I bought a coffee from a small shop nearby and tried to relax.
An hour felt long, but there was nothing else I could do about it now.
I opened a book I had brought along, just in case.
While I waited, I watched other people on the platform.
Some people ran too, just like me.
One man missed his train by even less time than I did, only a few seconds.
We looked at each other and both laughed a little.
He said this happens to him almost every week.
I told him it was my first time missing a train like this.
We talked while we waited, and the hour passed faster than I expected.
He told me a funny story about missing a flight once, in a different city entirely.
When my new train arrived, we said goodbye and got on different cars, still smiling about it.
Now, I always leave home fifteen minutes earlier than I think I need to.
One minute taught me a lesson that no clock ever could, and I haven't missed a train since.
I even arrive early enough now to buy coffee before boarding.
